walkthroughs.body_html:
The Norman Conquest 1065-1087 — a core area of GCSE History.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

The Norman Conquest 1065-1087 brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with The Norman Conquest 1065-1087.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: In what year was the Domesday Book completed?
What was the name of William's brutal northern campaign?
options: The Anarchy
Harrying of the North
Northern Crusade
York Suppression

mcqs.q: Why did William of Normandy claim the English throne in 1066?
options: Feudalism was a written constitution introduced by William in 1066.
William invaded because he was the strongest king in Europe and wanted more land.
He claimed Edward the Confessor had promised him the throne in 1051 and that Harold Godwinson had sworn an oath to support that claim in 1064.
William was Edward the Confessor's eldest son.

mcqs.q: Why did William the Conqueror commission the Domesday Book in 1086?
options: It was a census of the English population, like a modern one.
To record landholding and resources so he could assess taxation (geld), confirm Norman tenants' rights, and settle disputes over confiscated Anglo-Saxon estates.
It was a list of Anglo-Saxon rebels William wanted to execute.
William was Edward the Confessor's eldest son.

mcqs.q: How did the feudal system work in Norman England?
options: Feudalism meant peasants were slaves owned by the king.
It was a list of Anglo-Saxon rebels William wanted to execute.
Feudalism was a written constitution introduced by William in 1066.
The king granted land to tenants-in-chief in return for knight service; they in turn enfeoffed knights who held land in return for military service to their lord.
